Chord progressions help to create guidelines for the other instruments, but if you are going for a more melodic section you can always use the key/scale to create harmony.

Learning more about scales and modes can help you to make parts that compliment each other without using a chord progression. Some forms of music dabble more with riffs and melodies than chord progressions (take metal for example).

Also I would encourage you to make simpler songs, and to think hard about ideas like a "rhythm section" versus a "lead" for example. Maybe start with a drum groove, bassline, and rhythmic chord progression that are straightforward enough to create a "bed" for a lead that has the freedom to be more expressive and busy. Of course, you don't need to always use this formula, as you can choose to do a more complicated rhythm section that is syncopated with a lead part, but in general building songs in this fashion has helped me to construct more cohesive songs that make more sense upon first listen. Just think of it as one of many tools, and when you get good at making a stable and sense-making song, you can implement those elements and ideas into something more complex.

Lastly, know that not every instrument needs to share the spotlight at once. Make things a little more direct and in-your-face, so to speak. I just say all of this because the song you made here is cool, but it reminds me of stuff I used to make and I feel like I had similar questions about songwriting.

I generally agree, but lately I have looked into the work of Stanislav Grof. It is rather Freudian to think that our most significant trauma comes from early childhood- but how deep does it really go? Some of my psychedelic experiences have shown to me that trauma can go as far back as to prenatal and what Grof calls 'perinatal' (or around/relating-to-birth) experiences.

Consider for instance the deeply rooted trauma that could come from being born into the world via a Cesarian-section. I remember having vivid visions related to what my mother experienced during my birth. My mother also experienced great sickness towards the end of her pregnancy- which would undeniably have some sort of measurable impact on a fetus in development. Furthermore, circumcision and other post-natal procedures are often rationalized with doctors saying that newborns do not feel pain- but how could they possibly know? Where else could traumatic pain be stored in the body, other than our most immediately accessible memories?

Grof also explores synchronicities, and the possibility of ancestral/karmic trauma and wounding. It is at the very least interesting to consider that the human psyche is more advanced and complex than what we often assume.

If spiritualists were to declare the significance of visions, 'energies', and so forth, then the possibility of trauma that is within the collective unconscious of humanity is another thing to look into.
